rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Structural similarity to vitamin K; mild reduction in warfarin effect at high dose (≥100 mg/day). Effect is small but documented.
drug_class_hits.action: If you take warfarin, mention CoQ10 supplements to your prescriber. INR monitoring may need to be adjusted.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K and can slightly reduce how well warfarin works at higher doses.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.
drug_class_hits.action: CoQ10 100–300 mg/day may be used alongside statins, particularly if myopathy symptoms are present. Safe to co-administer.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 shares muscle or liver pathways with statins. If you take a statin, talk to your prescriber before adding CoQ10 and watch for new muscle aches.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects statin pathways — relevant to people on statin therapy.

rows.name: Proteases
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Structural similarity to vitamin K; mild reduction in warfarin effect at high dose (≥100 mg/day). Effect is small but documented.
drug_class_hits.action: If you take warfarin, mention CoQ10 supplements to your prescriber. INR monitoring may need to be adjusted.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K and can slightly reduce how well warfarin works at higher doses.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.
drug_class_hits.action: CoQ10 100–300 mg/day may be used alongside statins, particularly if myopathy symptoms are present. Safe to co-administer.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 shares muscle or liver pathways with statins. If you take a statin, talk to your prescriber before adding CoQ10 and watch for new muscle aches.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects statin pathways — relevant to people on statin therapy.

rows.name: Aspergillus niger
rows.notes: Broad-spectrum blend of enzymes sourced from fungal (Aspergillus) or botanical sources. Includes amylase, protease, lipase, cellulase, and often lactase. Fungal-derived enzymes are generally more acid-stable than animal-derived pancreatic enzymes, allowing activity across a wider pH range in the GI tract. DigeZyme (penta-enzyme complex) showed significant improvement in gastric/intestinal symptoms over 60 days in a clinical study. OTC supplements lack FDA regulation of enzyme potency and concentrations. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR (local action). 0.55 → null. Future activity-units scoring system.

rows.name: Amylase
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.

Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.

rows.name: Amylase

rows.name: Cellulase
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. rows.name: Coenzyme Q10
rows.notes: The label doesn't specify whether this is ubiquinol (active) or ubiquinone (oxidized), or what delivery format is used. Conservative score since it could be anything from premium crystal-free ubiquinol to cheap dry powder. Look for 'ubiquinol' or 'Kaneka QH' for a more accurate score. B32 audit 2026-04-25: CoQ10 class-poor.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

condition_hits.action: Limited data — discuss with your healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
condition_hits.alert_body: There isn't enough specific safety data to give a confident recommendation for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your obstetrician or pediatrician before using this supplement.
condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Structural similarity to vitamin K; mild reduction in warfarin effect at high dose (≥100 mg/day). Effect is small but documented.
drug_class_hits.action: If you take warfarin, mention CoQ10 supplements to your prescriber. INR monitoring may need to be adjusted.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K and can slightly reduce how well warfarin works at higher doses.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.
drug_class_hits.action: CoQ10 100–300 mg/day may be used alongside statins, particularly if myopathy symptoms are present. Safe to co-administer.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 shares muscle or liver pathways with statins. If you take a statin, talk to your prescriber before adding CoQ10 and watch for new muscle aches.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects statin pathways — relevant to people on statin therapy.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.informational_note: Pregnancy/lactation safety data is limited — clinician guidance recommended.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Structural similarity to vitamin K; mild reduction in warfarin effect at high dose (≥100 mg/day). Effect is small but documented.
drug_class_hits.action: If you take warfarin, mention CoQ10 supplements to your prescriber. INR monitoring may need to be adjusted.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K and can slightly reduce how well warfarin works at higher doses.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.
drug_class_hits.action: CoQ10 100–300 mg/day may be used alongside statins, particularly if myopathy symptoms are present. Safe to co-administer.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: CoEnzyme Q10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Structural similarity to vitamin K; mild reduction in warfarin effect at high dose (≥100 mg/day). Effect is small but documented.
drug_class_hits.action: If you take warfarin, mention CoQ10 supplements to your prescriber. INR monitoring may need to be adjusted.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K and can slightly reduce how well warfarin works at higher doses.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.
drug_class_hits.action: CoQ10 100–300 mg/day may be used alongside statins, particularly if myopathy symptoms are present. Safe to co-administer.
drug_class_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 shares muscle or liver pathways with statins. If you take a statin, talk to your prescriber before adding CoQ10 and watch for new muscle aches.
drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects statin pathways — relevant to people on statin therapy.

rows.name: Coenzyme B12
rows.absorption: mitochondrial coenzyme form; ~1-2% passive absorption at 1000 mcg dose
rows.notes: The mitochondrial active form of B12 (also called dibencozide or coenzyme B12). Essential for energy production in the Krebs cycle. The form your mitochondria actually use. Less common in supplements than methylcobalamin but equally important biologically. Evidence update 2026-04-25: Batch 10 audit verified PMIDs via PubMed eutils. ALL 5 supplied "well-known" reference PMIDs were misattributions (Carmel/Heaney/Shieh/Sato/Schurgers reassigned to verified PMIDs 18709891, 28187226, 23140417, 17158229, 11356998). D2 vs D3 difference corrected from "15.69 nmol/L" to verified 10.39 nmol/L (van den Heuvel 2024 PMID:37865222). MK-4 confirmed undetectable at nutritional doses (Sato 2012 PMID:23140417) — bio inflation flagged. B12 active-form bio inflation flagged: oral F is identical (~1-2% passive) across methyl/adenosyl/hydroxo/cyano forms; metabolic advantage is post-absorption. Dr Pham C2 sign-off: bio_score 14 → 8. Same passive 1-2% F as oral methylcobalamin.

condition_hits.mechanism: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is essential for DNA synthesis, cell division, and one-carbon metabolism. B12 deficiency elevates homocysteine via impaired methionine synthase activity, and hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), implantation failure, and embryotoxicity. Case-control studies document significantly lower serum B12 in women with recurrent miscarriage vs. controls (mean 197 vs 300 pg/mL, p=0.004 in one Syrian cohort; 178 vs 269 pg/mL, p<0.001 in a Polish cohort). B12 is a standard component of preconception care and prenatal vitamins. Optimizing B12 status before conception is associated with improved fertility outcomes and reduced RPL risk via homocysteine normalization.
condition_hits.action: Ensure adequate vitamin B12 status (serum B12 >400 pg/mL is optimal preconceptionally) when trying to conceive. Standard preconception supplementation: 2.4–6 mcg/day (adequate intake) up to higher doses if deficient. B12 supplementation is recommended as part of a comprehensive preconception vitamin regimen for all women TTC, and is particularly important for vegans, vegetarians, those with gastric conditions, or those on metformin (which reduces B12 absorption).
condition_hits.alert_body: Vitamin B12 used while trying to conceive is often continued through pregnancy as part of prenatal care. If you are planning pregnancy, discuss dosing of Vitamin B12 with your clinician.
condition_hits.informational_note: Vitamin B12 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Protease
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Coenzyme B12
rows.absorption: mitochondrial coenzyme form; ~1-2% passive absorption at 1000 mcg dose
rows.notes: The mitochondrial active form of B12 (also called dibencozide or coenzyme B12). Essential for energy production in the Krebs cycle. The form your mitochondria actually use. Less common in supplements than methylcobalamin but equally important biologically. Evidence update 2026-04-25: Batch 10 audit verified PMIDs via PubMed eutils. ALL 5 supplied "well-known" reference PMIDs were misattributions (Carmel/Heaney/Shieh/Sato/Schurgers reassigned to verified PMIDs 18709891, 28187226, 23140417, 17158229, 11356998). D2 vs D3 difference corrected from "15.69 nmol/L" to verified 10.39 nmol/L (van den Heuvel 2024 PMID:37865222). MK-4 confirmed undetectable at nutritional doses (Sato 2012 PMID:23140417) — bio inflation flagged. B12 active-form bio inflation flagged: oral F is identical (~1-2% passive) across methyl/adenosyl/hydroxo/cyano forms; metabolic advantage is post-absorption. Dr Pham C2 sign-off: bio_score 14 → 8. Same passive 1-2% F as oral methylcobalamin.

condition_hits.mechanism: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is essential for DNA synthesis, cell division, and one-carbon metabolism. B12 deficiency elevates homocysteine via impaired methionine synthase activity, and hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), implantation failure, and embryotoxicity. Case-control studies document significantly lower serum B12 in women with recurrent miscarriage vs. controls (mean 197 vs 300 pg/mL, p=0.004 in one Syrian cohort; 178 vs 269 pg/mL, p<0.001 in a Polish cohort). B12 is a standard component of preconception care and prenatal vitamins. Optimizing B12 status before conception is associated with improved fertility outcomes and reduced RPL risk via homocysteine normalization.
condition_hits.action: Ensure adequate vitamin B12 status (serum B12 >400 pg/mL is optimal preconceptionally) when trying to conceive. Standard preconception supplementation: 2.4–6 mcg/day (adequate intake) up to higher doses if deficient. B12 supplementation is recommended as part of a comprehensive preconception vitamin regimen for all women TTC, and is particularly important for vegans, vegetarians, those with gastric conditions, or those on metformin (which reduces B12 absorption).
condition_hits.alert_body: Vitamin B12 used while trying to conceive is often continued through pregnancy as part of prenatal care. If you are planning pregnancy, discuss dosing of Vitamin B12 with your clinician.
condition_hits.informational_note: Vitamin B12 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.mechanism: B12 is an essential nutrient throughout pregnancy and lactation. Deficiency is associated with neural tube defects, developmental delay, and recurrent pregnancy loss via hyperhomocysteinemia. Standard prenatal vitamins contain B12; supplementation should continue throughout pregnancy and during breastfeeding.
condition_hits.action: B12 supplementation during pregnancy is part of standard prenatal care. Vegans and those with malabsorption (pernicious anemia, gastric surgery, metformin use) need higher supplemental doses.
condition_hits.alert_body: B12 is essential throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding, and supplementation started pre-conception should continue. If you are pregnant or nursing, discuss dosing with your obstetrician.
condition_hits.informational_note: B12 is part of standard prenatal support — relevant to anyone pregnant or breastfeeding.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.

rows.absorption: Oil-based softgel; ~3% absolute F; take with fatty meal
rows.notes: Standard ubiquinone dissolved in oil inside a softgel capsule. The oil base helps dissolve the CoQ10 crystals, improving absorption modestly over dry powder. A reliable mid-tier form and the most common quality CoQ10 delivery. Always take with a fat-containing meal for best results. Citation correction 2026-04-25: "~2.3× better than dry powder" specific fold-change is not in López-Lluch 2019 (PMID:30153575). That paper confirms oil-softgel as superior by AUC ranking but does not report this specific multiplier. Absolute F ~3% per Bhagavan 2006 class baseline. Dr Pham C1 sign-off (PD-respect): bio=11 retained; F~3% reflects PK reality.

rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. rows.name: Papain
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Lactase
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.

rows.notes: The label doesn't specify whether this is ubiquinol (active) or ubiquinone (oxidized), or what delivery format is used. condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

drug_class_hits.mechanism: Statins deplete endogenous CoQ10 by blocking the mevalonate pathway. CoQ10 supplementation is commonly used to mitigate statin-associated myopathy. No adverse pharmacokinetic interaction between CoQ10 and statins has been demonstrated.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

rows.name: Coenzyme Q-10
rows.absorption: Crystalline CoQ10; ~2% absolute F; slow & limited absorption
rows.notes: The basic oxidized form of CoQ10 in a standard capsule or tablet. Your body converts it to active ubiquinol after absorption. Well-studied and affordable, but the crystalline structure limits how much dissolves in your gut. Taking it with a fat-containing meal significantly improves absorption. Produced by Kaneka (the world's largest CoQ10 manufacturer). Evidence update 2026-04-25: Bhagavan & Chopra 2006 (PMID:16551570) established the class baseline — oral CoQ10 absorption is slow (Tmax ~6 h, t½ ~33 h) and limited (~2% absolute F) due to lipophilicity and large molecular weight (863 Da).

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Coenzyme Q10
rows.notes: The label doesn't specify whether this is ubiquinol (active) or ubiquinone (oxidized), or what delivery format is used. Conservative score since it could be anything from premium crystal-free ubiquinol to cheap dry powder. Look for 'ubiquinol' or 'Kaneka QH' for a more accurate score. B32 audit 2026-04-25: CoQ10 class-poor.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

drug_class_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 may affect INR at high doses — relevant to anyone on warfarin.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) is involved in mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cardiac myocytes. Supplementation has shown modest benefit in heart failure (improved ejection fraction and symptom class in Q-SYMBIO trial). However, CoQ10 may interfere with anticoagulation therapy (warfarin), an important consideration in cardiac patients.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 may be beneficial in heart failure under clinician guidance. Monitor INR closely if on warfarin, as CoQ10 has been associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 3.69 in longitudinal study). Discuss with cardiologist before initiating.
condition_hits.alert_headline: Discuss CoQ10 with your heart clinician
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 has been studied in some heart conditions, but it should not replace prescribed heart medication. Ask your clinician if it fits your care plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 can affect cardiovascular pathways — relevant to people with heart conditions.

condition_hits.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking not only cholesterol synthesis but also the mevalonate pathway used to synthesize CoQ10. Plasma and muscle CoQ10 levels are measurably reduced by statin therapy. CoQ10 depletion is proposed as a contributing mechanism to statin-induced myopathy.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–300 mg/day) is commonly used to address statin-induced muscle symptoms. It is considered safe to combine. Discuss with prescriber whether supplementation is warranted based on symptoms.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly discussed alongside statin therapy because statins may reduce CoQ10 levels. Evidence for symptom benefit is mixed. If you take a statin, ask your clinician about CoQ10.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 affects lipid pathways — relevant to people managing high cholesterol.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

condition_hits.mechanism: CoQ10 is an essential mitochondrial antioxidant. Oocyte quality declines with age partly due to reduced mitochondrial CoQ10 availability and impaired ATP production. Ben-Meir et al. (2015, Aging Cell) demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice, prevented premature ovarian failure in Pdss2-deficient animals, and improved meiotic spindle integrity. A 2024 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (Shang et al.) found CoQ10 improved retrieved oocyte count, high-quality embryo rates, and clinical pregnancy rates in women with ovarian aging, with optimal effect at 30 mg/day for 3 months before ovarian stimulation in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.
condition_hits.action: CoQ10 supplementation (100–600 mg/day, commonly 200–400 mg/day) may support oocyte quality during the preconception period, especially in women over 35 or those with diminished ovarian reserve. Safe to use during TTC. Discontinue when pregnancy is confirmed to return to standard prenatal supplement regimen.
condition_hits.alert_body: CoQ10 is commonly studied in fertility care, especially around oocyte mitochondrial function and ovarian aging. Evidence is still evolving, so use it as part of a clinician-guided plan.
condition_hits.informational_note: CoQ10 is continued under clinician guidance — relevant to people planning pregnancy.

rows.name: Protease 6
rows.notes: Targeted individual enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase, bromelain, papain, serrapeptase, lactase, cellulase, etc.) designed to break down specific food components in the GI lumen. Enzymes work locally — systemic absorption is NOT the relevant metric; GI stability and enzyme activity delivery matter. Without enteric coating, many enzymes are partially denatured by stomach acid (~30-50% survival). OTC enzyme supplements are not FDA-regulated and enzyme concentrations are not guaranteed (Johns Hopkins Medicine). Well-characterized branded forms (DigeZyme, ProHydrolase) have more reliable potency. Dr Pham E3 sign-off: CATEGORY ERROR. 0.40 → null.
